e1.spell.plurals.explain: cat -> cats. We add -s to make it plural.
box -> boxes. Words ending in s, x, ch, sh or zz add -es.

e1.spell.plurals.hint: Say it out loud. Can you hear the extra 'iz' sound?
e1.spell.plurals.explain: bus -> buses. Words ending in s add -es.
brush -> brushes. Words ending in sh add -es.

e1.spell.plurals.hint: You only need one extra letter.

e1.spell.plurals.explain: church -> churches. Words ending in ch add -es.
fox -> foxes, because it ends in x.

e1.spell.plurals.prompt: Which word already means more than one?
e1.spell.plurals.hint: Look for the -s on the end.
e1.spell.plurals.explain: shells means more than one shell.

e1.spell.prefix-un.explain: un- at the front of a word means 'not'. unhappy means not happy.

e1.spell.prefix-un.prompt: The shoelace came ... . Which word fits?
e1.spell.prefix-un.hint: The lace was done up, now it is not.
e1.spell.prefix-un.explain: undone means not done up any more.
un- + fair = unfair, which means not fair.
unwell means not well, or a bit poorly.
unlock means to undo the locking, so the door opens.
untidy means not tidy — a messy room!

e1.spell.prefix-un.hint: un- always goes at the front of the word.
e1.spell.prefix-un.explain: un- is a prefix, so it goes at the start: unlocked.

e1.spell.suffix-ing-ed.explain: jump + ed = jumped. We use -ed for something that already happened.

e1.spell.suffix-ing-ed.prompt: Right now I am ... a picture. (paint)
e1.spell.suffix-ing-ed.explain: paint + ing = painting. We use -ing for something happening now.

e1.spell.suffix-ing-ed.hint: Just add the letters. Nothing changes.

e1.spell.suffix-ing-ed.prompt: Last night we ... to stay up late. (want)
e1.spell.suffix-ing-ed.hint: Last night is in the past, so add -ed.
Add three letters: i, n, g.

e1.spell.suffix-ing-ed.prompt: The dog is ... at the postman. (bark)
e1.spell.suffix-ing-ed.explain: bark + ing = barking, because it is happening now.

e1.spell.suffix-ing-ed.prompt: Which word is in the past?
e1.spell.suffix-ing-ed.explain: walked has -ed on the end, so it already happened.

e1.spell.suffix-er-est.prompt: This tree is tall. That tree is even ... .
e1.spell.suffix-er-est.explain: When we compare two things we add -er: taller.

e1.spell.suffix-er-est.prompt: Out of all the trees, this one is the ... .
e1.spell.suffix-er-est.hint: The very top one out of many uses -est.
e1.spell.suffix-er-est.explain: For the very most out of all of them we add -est: tallest.
smallest means the very smallest of them all.

e1.spell.suffix-er-est.prompt: A mouse is ... than an elephant.
e1.spell.suffix-er-est.explain: We compare two things with -er: smaller.

e1.spell.suffix-er-est.hint: Add three letters: e, s, t.

choices: My bag is heavier than yours.
My bag is heaviest than yours.
My bag is heavy than yours.
My bag is heavyer than yours.
e1.spell.suffix-er-est.answer: My bag is heavier than yours.
e1.spell.suffix-er-est.hint: The word 'than' tells you two things are compared.
e1.spell.suffix-er-est.explain: Comparing two things uses -er, and heavy changes its y to i: heavier.

e1.spell.suffix-er-est.hint: Nothing changes at the end of soft.

e1.spell.tricky-words.hint: It does not sound the way it looks.
e1.spell.tricky-words.explain: said is a tricky word. It sounds like 'sed' but is spelt s-a-i-d.

e1.spell.tricky-words.hint: Big Elephants Can Always Understand Small Elephants.
There is a hidden 'i' after the r.
e1.spell.tricky-words.explain: friend has 'i' before 'e': f-r-i-e-n-d. A friend is there to the end.

e1.spell.tricky-words.hint: This one means a place: over there.
e1.spell.tricky-words.explain: there is spelt t-h-e-r-e. It contains the word 'here'.

e1.spell.tricky-words.hint: It sounds like 'woz' but is not spelt that way.
It has a silent h after the c.
It starts like the number one.

e1.phon.digraphs.prompt: Which two letters make the sound at the start of 'ship'?
e1.phon.digraphs.explain: 'sh' makes one sound, like asking someone to be quiet.

e1.phon.digraphs.prompt: Which word starts with the 'ch' sound?
e1.phon.digraphs.hint: Listen for the sound a train makes: ch-ch-ch.

e1.phon.digraphs.prompt: Which two letters make the sound at the end of 'bath'?
e1.phon.digraphs.hint: Poke your tongue out a little to say it.
e1.phon.digraphs.explain: 'th' makes one sound at the end of bath.

e1.phon.digraphs.prompt: Which word has the 'ng' sound at the end?
e1.phon.digraphs.hint: Say each word and listen to the very end.

e1.phon.digraphs.prompt: How do you spell the word for a thing you talk into?
e1.phon.digraphs.hint: The 'f' sound is made by 'ph' here.
e1.phon.digraphs.explain: phone uses 'ph' to make the 'f' sound.
rain has the 'ai' digraph making an 'ay' sound.

e1.phon.digraphs.prompt: Which word has the 'oo' sound as in 'moon'?
Which three letters make the sound in the middle of 'night'?
e1.phon.digraphs.hint: It is a trigraph — three letters, one sound.
e1.phon.digraphs.explain: 'igh' makes the long 'i' sound in night.

e1.phon.digraphs.prompt: Which word starts with a 'wh' sound?

choices: The cat sat on the mat.
the cat sat on the mat.
The cat sat on the mat
the cat sat on the mat
e1.punct.capitals-stops.answer: The cat sat on the mat.
e1.punct.capitals-stops.hint: Sentences start with a capital and end with a full stop.
e1.punct.capitals-stops.explain: A sentence needs a capital letter at the start and a full stop at the end.

e1.punct.capitals-stops.prompt: Which word needs a capital letter?
e1.punct.capitals-stops.hint: Names of places always get a capital.
e1.punct.capitals-stops.explain: London is the name of a place, so it needs a capital L.
The sentence starts with a capital M, Sam gets a capital S, and it ends with a full stop.

e1.punct.capitals-stops.prompt: Which letter should always be a capital when it means 'me'?
e1.punct.capitals-stops.hint: It is just one letter long.
e1.punct.capitals-stops.explain: The word I is always a capital letter.

e1.punct.capitals-stops.prompt: How many full stops does this need? 'I have a dog I have a cat'
e1.punct.capitals-stops.hint: Count how many separate ideas there are.
e1.punct.capitals-stops.explain: There are two sentences, so two full stops: I have a dog. I have a cat.

e1.punct.capitals-stops.prompt: Which word needs a capital letter?
e1.punct.capitals-stops.hint: Days of the week are names.
e1.punct.capitals-stops.explain: Monday is the name of a day, so it needs a capital M.

e1.punct.capitals-stops.hint: Only the first word and names need capitals.
e1.punct.capitals-stops.explain: Capital W at the start, full stop at the end, and no other capitals needed.

e1.punct.capitals-stops.prompt: What goes at the end of a telling sentence?
e1.punct.capitals-stops.explain: A telling sentence (a statement) ends with a full stop.

e1.punct.capitals-stops.prompt: Which word needs a capital letter?
e1.punct.capitals-stops.hint: It is the name of a country.
e1.punct.capitals-stops.explain: England is a name, so it needs a capital E.

e1.punct.capitals-stops.hint: The word I is always a capital.
e1.punct.capitals-stops.explain: I is always a capital, and the sentence ends with a full stop.

e1.punct.question-exclaim.prompt: What punctuation ends this sentence? 'What is your name'
e1.punct.question-exclaim.explain: A sentence that asks something ends with a question mark.

e1.punct.question-exclaim.prompt: What punctuation ends this sentence? 'Look out'
e1.punct.question-exclaim.hint: It is a shout or a surprise.
e1.punct.question-exclaim.explain: An exclamation mark shows strong feeling, like a shout.

e1.punct.question-exclaim.hint: Questions often start with words like where, what or who.
e1.punct.question-exclaim.explain: Where is my bag? asks something, so it is a question.

e1.punct.question-exclaim.prompt: What punctuation ends this sentence? 'How old are you'
e1.punct.question-exclaim.explain: It is asking something, so it needs a question mark.

e1.punct.question-exclaim.prompt: Which sentence needs an exclamation mark?
e1.punct.question-exclaim.hint: Which one has the most feeling?
e1.punct.question-exclaim.explain: That is amazing! shows strong feeling.

e1.punct.question-exclaim.prompt: Which word often starts a question?
e1.punct.question-exclaim.hint: Think of the question words: who, what, where, when, why, how.

e1.punct.question-exclaim.prompt: What punctuation ends this sentence? 'I love ice cream'
e1.punct.question-exclaim.hint: It shows a big happy feeling.
e1.punct.question-exclaim.explain: An exclamation mark shows strong feeling: I love ice cream!

e1.punct.question-exclaim.hint: Check the capital letter and the ending.
e1.punct.question-exclaim.explain: It starts with a capital C and, because it asks something, ends with a question mark.

e1.gram.joining.prompt: Join the sentences: 'I had toast' + 'I had juice'.
e1.gram.joining.explain: We use 'and' to join two ideas that go together.

e1.gram.joining.prompt: Which word joins these? 'I ran fast ___ I still lost.'
e1.gram.joining.hint: The second part is a surprise.
e1.gram.joining.explain: 'but' joins two ideas that do not quite match.

e1.gram.joining.prompt: Which word fits? 'Would you like milk ___ water?'
e1.gram.joining.hint: There is a choice between two things.
e1.gram.joining.explain: 'or' is used when there is a choice.
'and' sits between the two things being joined.

e1.gram.joining.prompt: Which word fits? 'It was raining ___ we stayed inside.'
Join these with 'and': 'The dog barked' + 'the cat ran'.
choices: The dog barked and the cat ran.
The dog and barked the cat ran.
And the dog barked the cat ran.
The dog barked the cat and ran.
e1.gram.joining.answer: The dog barked and the cat ran.
e1.gram.joining.hint: Put 'and' in the middle, between the two parts.
e1.gram.joining.explain: 'and' joins the two parts of the sentence in the middle.

e1.gram.joining.prompt: Which word joins these? 'I wanted to play ___ it was bedtime.'
e1.gram.joining.hint: The two parts disagree with each other.
e1.gram.joining.explain: 'but' shows that the second part is unexpected.

e1.gram.joining.prompt: Which sentence has TWO ideas joined together?
choices: I ate my lunch and played outside.
e1.gram.joining.answer: I ate my lunch and played outside.
e1.gram.joining.explain: This sentence joins 'I ate my lunch' and 'played outside' with 'and'.
